Yeah, this is a form of data leakage that comes from your computer working the way computers work, basically. Disclaimer, I have not established this as factually true by reading through code and actually debugging--I just happen to be a software engineer, and this behavior looks like something very common that I see.

We like to imagine computers' memory as something like a piece of paper, that can be blank, or not. But that's not really an apt metaphor. It's better to think of computers' memory as a bunch of coins lined up end-to-end, and those coins are either 'tails' or 'heads'. When your RAM is fully discharged, and there is no electricity in it at all, each of the bits is in the 'zero' state. Likewise, in your hard drive, the 'bits' are made up of metal, and the metal has a magnetic field that's either up-ish or down-ish.

The key thing to understand here is that it isn't especially meaningful to talk about "erasing" memory contents. You can replace them--for example, if you have a region of memory you don't want to use anymore, you could over--write it. You could over-write it with all zeros, if you like. You could just as easily over-write it with all ones, or with alternating ones-and-zeros.

What happens most commonly, is you do none of these things. Most commonly, you simply tell the computer's operating system, "Hey, I don't need this anymore." and then, whatever data was there, it just stays there. At some point in the future, the computer will hand that memory over to a different process. At this point, it's the responsibility of whoever "gets" the memory to clear it or set it up as they need.

Sometimes, as you're seeing with Chrome, the same chunk of memory gets handed back to the same process. And sometimes, there is data leftover in there--in this case, an image of your Incognito window. So, ultimately, if I'm correct--then as soon as you load a page in your new chrome window, and it renders a view of that page, it over-writes the Incognito content you see and then it's gone.
